50	 Introduction
51	 Patellar tendinopathy (PT) is an extremely common musculoskeletal issue in elite athletes
52	 competing in jumping sports where reports of prevalence reach between 32% (basketball) and 44.6%
53	 (volleyball), whereas in body weight supported sports such as cycling the incidence of PT is low (Lian et
54	 al., 2005). Interestingly, sub-elite athletes report significantly lower patellar tendinopathy (14.4% for
55	 volleyball), suggesting that the volume or intensity of loading contributes to the development of this
56	 chronic problem (Hagglund et al., 2011; Janssen et al., 2015). Patellar tendinopathy is especially common
57	 in professional basketball due to the high playing load and intensity. In a preliminary report from the
58	 Australian National Basketball League, 52.3% of players reported patellar tendon pain that limited
59	Downloaded by t_lambrinides@yahoo.com on 11/16/18
60	 performance (Hannington et al., 2017), suggesting that the prevalence of this injury is high at the elite
61	 level.
62	 Typically, severe chronic patellar tendinopathy can be visualized by MRI as an increase in signal
63	 intensity at the inferior pole of the patella (Johnson et al., 1996), suggesting that is develops from an injury
64	 to the proximal enthesis. In non-elite athletes, patellar tendinopathy is treated with rest and cryotherapy
65	 with limited success (Schwartz et al., 2015). Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are equivocal
66	 as to their effect on tendinopathy (Weiler, 1992). Indeed, recent work suggests that NSAIDs may not even
67	 be delivered to human tendons sufficiently to alter gene expression (Heinemeier et al., 2017).
68	 One of the major issues surrounding patellar tendinopathy is that stress shielding can occur with
69	 loading (Almekinders et al., 2002), specifically at the insertion/origin regions (Orchard et al., 2004). Stress
70	 shielding is most commonly associated with the implantation of prosthetics within bone (Sumner, 2015).
71	 Essentially, the stronger metal components of the implant shield the neighboring bone from load (stress)
72	 resulting in more of the load being transmitted through the metal and subsequent loss of the “unloaded”
73	 native bone (Sumner, 2015). By analogy, healthy collagen can shield weaker or injured regions within the
74	 tendon resulting in unloading and a subsequent decrease in collagen content and orientation within the
75	  “Stress Relaxation and Targeted Nutrition to Treat Patellar Tendinopathy” by Baar K
76	 International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism
77	 © 2018 Human Kinetics, Inc.
78	 injured region (Docking et al., 2016). The change in collagen content and orientation within the injured
79	 region is further associated with an increase in proteoglycans and water (Samiric et al., 2009), suggesting
80	 that the stress-shielded region of the tendon may be placed under a compressive load as the stronger
81	 collagen fibers squeeze (compress) the shielded region (Docking et al., 2013; Majima et al., 2000).
82	 One way to overcome stress shielding is to take advantage of stress relaxation within the tendon
83	 (Atkinson et al., 1999). Stress relaxation is a fundamental property of viscoelastic tissues like tendons,
84	 where force within a tendon decreases over time when a static load is applied and the tendon is held at a
85	 constant length(Atkinson et al., 1999). Essentially, this means that when a tendon is loaded using isometric
86	 contractions the collagen fibers/fibrils/fascicles progressively relax over time, eventually reaching a steady
87	Downloaded by t_lambrinides@yahoo.com on 11/16/18
88	 state. As the collagen fibers/fibrils/fascicles relax, stress shielding within the tendon should decrease and
89	 a directional mechanical signal should be imparted to the injured region. Consistent with this hypothesis,
90	 isometric loading protocols decrease pain in high level athletes with tendinopathies (Rio et al., 2015; van
91	 Ark et al., 2016); however, whether a consistent program of isometric loading can improve the quality of
92	 the injured tendon has yet to be demonstrated.
93	 On top of the positive effects of loading on tendon health, we have recently shown that nutrition
94	 can positively affect collagen synthesis in musculoskeletal tissues (Shaw et al., 2017). Briefly, we
95	 demonstrated that supplementing with 15 grams of gelatin, one hour before loading, resulted in an
96	 increase in whole body collagen synthesis and increased mechanics and collagen content of human
97	 engineered ligaments (Shaw et al., 2017). These data suggest that supplementing with gelatin can increase
98	 collagen synthesis. Improving collagen synthesis in stress shielded tendon might be important since
99	 immobilization for even short periods (10 days) has been shown to reduce tendon collagen synthesis by
100	 up to 50% and the decline in collagen synthesis continues out to 23 days (de Boer et al., 2007). Even
101	 though the decrease in collagen synthesis was not associated with a decrease in patellar tendon cross-

103	 International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism
104	 © 2018 Human Kinetics, Inc.
105	 sectional area, the tendon did show decreased functional performance (de Boer et al., 2007), suggesting
106	 that decreased collagen synthesis is associated with impaired tendon function.
107	 This paper, presents a case study of a professional basketball player with chronic patellar
108	 tendinopathy. The player was placed on a program that combined gelatin ingestion and stress relaxation
109	 loading as part of a rehabilitation protocol. Of note, even with an extensive playing and training schedule,
110	 the protocol significantly decreased MRI reactivity, increased the thickness of the mid-substance of the
111	 patellar tendon, and diminished pain. The loading and nutrition protocol presented here therefore could
112	 be one component of a rehabilitation protocol to improve functional outcomes in elite athletes.

130	 Overview of interventions
131	 After being informed of the purpose of the study and of all associated risks, the player gave written
132	 consent. The study was performed in accordance with the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki
133	 and the University of California Davis Institutional Review Board.
134	 In-Season Loading Volume
135	 As the player was part of the active team, he participated in more than 50 games per season across two
136	 season averaging more than 20 minutes per contest. On top of game loading, he also participated in an
137	 average of 3 organized practices per week as well as a structured strength training program overseen by
138	 an elite strength and conditioning coach while being monitored by a rehabilitation specialist,
139	Downloaded by t_lambrinides@yahoo.com on 11/16/18
140	 physiotherapist, and sport medicine doctor.
141	 Stress Relaxation Loading
142	 The patellar tendon targeted training program consisted of mid-range isometric holds for 2 open
143	 chain (leg extension, and leg press) and one closed chain (Spanish squats) exercise. Both the weight lifted
144	 and the duration of the isometric hold progressively increased over the 18 months in the program. The
145	 isometric holds started at 10 seconds and progressively increased by 5 seconds and reached a peak of 30
146	 seconds 6 months into the program. The stress relaxation program was performed twice a week through
147	 pre-season, in-season, and off-season workouts. The athlete was asked to perform 1-3 sets of 2-4
148	 repetitions of single leg, mid-range isometric holds for leg extension, leg press, or Spanish squats. The
149	 holds were performed at >80% of 1 repetition max (1RM) and 1RM was evaluated every other month. The
150	 30 second isometric holds were used because the force in patellar tendon sections drops by 60% by 30
151	 seconds with only a further 10% decrease by 180 seconds (Atkinson et al., 1999). The length of the session
152	 (~10 minutes from start to finish) was used because we had previously found that short periods of loading

156	 (5-10 minutes) were optimal for stimulating the cellular response to load and increasing collagen synthesis
157	 (Paxton et al., 2012).
158	 Nutrition intervention
159	 Normal dietary intake for the player was not tracked, nor did the player report changes in dietary
160	 intake over the length of the study. One hour before the patellar tendon targeted training program, the
161	 athlete consumed 15 grams of gelatin with ~225 mg vitamin C. The supplement consisted of commercial
162	 baking gelatin (Great Lakes unflavored beef gelatin) in 16oz of orange juice (containing ~225mg vitamin
163	 C). The amount of gelatin was based on our previous work showing that 15 grams of gelatin increased
164	 load-dependent collagen synthesis (Shaw et al., 2017). The timing of nutrients prior to exercise was

166	 designed to enhance nutrient delivery to the injured tendon and take advantage of cellular processes
167	 activated by the exercise stimulus to maximize collagen synthesis.
168	 Compliance with the loading and nutrition program was greater than 95% in season and because
169	 of the early success the athlete maintained approximately this level of compliance in the offseason.

194	 Imaging and pain
195	 Follow up MRI images were performed after a year in the program (15 months after the first MRI)
196	 and a further 6 months later, after the player had been on the program for ~18 months. The MRI images
197	 following 12 and 18 months into the program showed a progressive decrease in MRI reactivity at the
198	 inferior pole of the patella in both the sagittal T1 weighted images (Figure 1) and the axial SPAIR images
199	 (Figure 2). At the time of the third scan, a blinded orthopedic surgeon declared the patellar tendon normal.
200	 The reduction of reactivity at the inferior pole of the patella was accompanied by a decrease in the
201	 diameter of the patellar tendon at the proximal enthesis from 10.8mm at scan 1 to 8.7 and 8.16mm in
202	 scans 2 and 3, respectively. The decrease in the thickness of the proximal end of the patellar tendon was
203	 accompanied by an increase in the thickness at the mid-point of the tendon. The diameter of the midpoint
204	 of the patellar tendon progressively increased from 5.74 (scan 1), to 6.16 (scan 2) and then 6.29 (scan 3)
205	 mm and this was accompanied by a decrease in T1 and T2 reactivity (not shown). Therefore, the proximal
206	 end of the tendon decreased ~25%, whereas the middle of the tendon hypertrophied ~10%. Beyond the

212	 Reflections
213	 The goal of this case study was to determine whether a targeted loading and nutritional program
214	 could enhance outcomes of a patellar tendinopathy rehabilitation program. Specifically, we used a loading
215	 program that maximized stress relaxation (long isometric holds) in the hopes of providing a uniaxial tensile
216	 load to the injured region of the patellar tendon. Together with the stress relaxation loading, we primed
217	 the athlete with 15 grams of gelatin containing 225mg of vitamin C so that once the cells were activated
218	 by the load they had would have the substrates necessary to increase collagen synthesis. The major results
219	Downloaded by t_lambrinides@yahoo.com on 11/16/18
220	 of the program were a decrease in pain and tenderness that corresponded with a significant decrease in
221	 MRI reactivity at the inferior pole of the patella and an increase in mid-substance patellar tendon
222	 thickness.
223	 Stress relaxation is a fundamental property of viscoelastic materials like tendons and ligaments
224	 (Kjaer, 2004). Basically, as the tissue is loaded water is squeezed out and structures, such as fascicles and
225	 sub-fascicular components of the tendon slide relative to each other resulting in a progressive decrease
226	 in the tension within the tendon at a given length (Atkinson et al., 1999; Magnusson et al., 1997). In the
227	 human patellar tendon, two important observations about stress relaxation were first made by Atkinson
228	 and her colleagues (Atkinson et al., 1999). First, stress relaxation is bigger when larger parts of a tendon
229	 are loaded. This is important since it suggests that intrinsic differences in the strength of different fascicle
230	 or sub-fascicle regions are exposed during stress relaxation. In the current case, this is potentially
231	 important since it suggests that stronger regions of the tendon may relax early in the process and
232	 weaker/damaged regions of the tendon may be forced to take on more of the load as stress relaxation
233	 progresses. Since directional loading is fundamentally required for high degrees of collagen synthesis and
234	 matrix alignment (Kapacee et al., 2008), this suggests that stress relaxation can be used to provide a
235	  “Stress Relaxation and Targeted Nutrition to Treat Patellar Tendinopathy” by Baar K
236	 International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism
237	 © 2018 Human Kinetics, Inc.
238	 tensile stimulus to damaged regions of the collagen matrix to promote directional collagen synthesis. The
239	 second important observation by Atkinson and colleagues (Atkinson et al., 1999) was that stress-
240	 relaxation reaches ~60% within 30 seconds and continues only a further 10% more up to 180 seconds.
241	 This suggests that heavy isometric holds lasting 30 seconds will be sufficient to provide a similar degree
242	 of stress relaxation as holds lasting 6-times longer. Therefore, the rationale for the loading paradigm was
243	 to use stress relaxation to provide a tensile load to the cells within the damaged central core of the
244	 proximal patellar tendon.
245	 As important as tensile loading is to collagen synthesis, recent work from our group (Shaw et al.,
246	 2017) and others (Clark et al., 2008; McAlindon et al., 2011; Oesser et al., 1999) suggests that collagen
247	Downloaded by t_lambrinides@yahoo.com on 11/16/18
248	 synthesis can be enhanced by supplementing the diet with gelatin or hydrolyzed collagen. Specifically, we
249	 have previously shown that providing 15 grams of gelatin together with ~50mg of vitamin C an hour before
250	 loading resulted in an increase in collagen synthesis relative to a placebo or 5-gram dose of gelatin (Shaw
251	 et al., 2017). Therefore, for this case study we had the athlete consume 15 grams of gelatin within an
252	 orange juice slurry (containing ~225mg of vitamin C) one hour before the stress relaxation training. Even
253	 though we do not have a control group for this intervention, we have growing evidence that specific amino
254	 acids within the gelatin provide a stimulus to the cells of a tendon or ligament to increase collagen
255	 synthesis. Coupled with the directional tensile load, the added amino acids may be necessary to support
256	 the increase in collagen synthesis. However, much more work is needed before we can definitively
257	 understand the role of gelatin in the recovery described in this case study.
258	 As with any intervention with elite athletes, the intervention can only be effective if there is buy
259	 in from the player. In this case, the injury was sufficiently painful that the player was willing to drink the
260	 slurry and perform the loading paradigm twice a week. When the treatment showed success, the player
261	 quickly became a major advocate of the program within the team. Currently, any player with symptoms
262	 of patellar or other forms of tendinopathy quickly opts into the program and now most members of the
263	  “Stress Relaxation and Targeted Nutrition to Treat Patellar Tendinopathy” by Baar K
264	 International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism
265	 © 2018 Human Kinetics, Inc.
266	 team preform a form of prehab using the gelatin and stress relaxation loading along with their regular
267	 training. Even though we have not quantified musculoskeletal injuries before and after the intervention,
268	 reports suggest that visits to the training room and non-contact musculoskeletal injuries within the team
269	 have dropped.
270	 Tendinopathies are multifactorial in nature and central core tendinopathies are particularly
271	 difficult to prevent and treat in an elite population. We hope that the program reported here can provide
272	 a starting place for treating these debilitating injuries.

  “Stress Relaxation and Targeted Nutrition to Treat Patellar Tendinopathy” by Baar K
 International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism
 © 2018 Human Kinetics, Inc.
 Abstract
 Patellar tendinopathy is one of the most common afflictions in jumping sports. This case study outlines
 the rehabilitation of a professional basketball player diagnosed by MRI with a central core patellar
 tendinopathy within the proximal enthesis. The player undertook a nutrition and strength based
 rehabilitation program combining gelatin ingestion and heavy isometric loading of the patella designed to
 produce significant stress relaxation as part of their competition schedule and a whole body training plan.
 On follow up one and a half years into the program an independent orthopedic surgeon declared the
 tendon normal on MRI. Importantly, the improved MRI results were associated with a decrease in pain
 and improved performance. This case study provides evidence that a nutritional intervention combined
Downloaded by t_lambrinides@yahoo.com on 11/16/18
 with a rehabilitation program that uses stress relaxation can improve clinical outcomes in elite athletes.
 Keywords: Exercise, Tendon, Jumper’s Knee, Loading, Rehabilitation
  “Stress Relaxation and Targeted Nutrition to Treat Patellar Tendinopathy” by Baar K
 International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism
 © 2018 Human Kinetics, Inc.
 Introduction
 Patellar tendinopathy (PT) is an extremely common musculoskeletal issue in elite athletes
 competing in jumping sports where reports of prevalence reach between 32% (basketball) and 44.6%
 (volleyball), whereas in body weight supported sports such as cycling the incidence of PT is low (Lian et
 al., 2005). Interestingly, sub-elite athletes report significantly lower patellar tendinopathy (14.4% for
 volleyball), suggesting that the volume or intensity of loading contributes to the development of this
 chronic problem (Hagglund et al., 2011; Janssen et al., 2015). Patellar tendinopathy is especially common
 in professional basketball due to the high playing load and intensity. In a preliminary report from the
 Australian National Basketball League, 52.3% of players reported patellar tendon pain that limited
Downloaded by t_lambrinides@yahoo.com on 11/16/18
 performance (Hannington et al., 2017), suggesting that the prevalence of this injury is high at the elite
 level.
 Typically, severe chronic patellar tendinopathy can be visualized by MRI as an increase in signal
 intensity at the inferior pole of the patella (Johnson et al., 1996), suggesting that is develops from an injury
 to the proximal enthesis. In non-elite athletes, patellar tendinopathy is treated with rest and cryotherapy
 with limited success (Schwartz et al., 2015). Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are equivocal
 as to their effect on tendinopathy (Weiler, 1992). Indeed, recent work suggests that NSAIDs may not even
 be delivered to human tendons sufficiently to alter gene expression (Heinemeier et al., 2017).
 One of the major issues surrounding patellar tendinopathy is that stress shielding can occur with
 loading (Almekinders et al., 2002), specifically at the insertion/origin regions (Orchard et al., 2004). Stress
 shielding is most commonly associated with the implantation of prosthetics within bone (Sumner, 2015).
 Essentially, the stronger metal components of the implant shield the neighboring bone from load (stress)
 resulting in more of the load being transmitted through the metal and subsequent loss of the “unloaded”
 native bone (Sumner, 2015). By analogy, healthy collagen can shield weaker or injured regions within the
 tendon resulting in unloading and a subsequent decrease in collagen content and orientation within the
  “Stress Relaxation and Targeted Nutrition to Treat Patellar Tendinopathy” by Baar K
 International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism
 © 2018 Human Kinetics, Inc.
 injured region (Docking et al., 2016). The change in collagen content and orientation within the injured
 region is further associated with an increase in proteoglycans and water (Samiric et al., 2009), suggesting
 that the stress-shielded region of the tendon may be placed under a compressive load as the stronger
 collagen fibers squeeze (compress) the shielded region (Docking et al., 2013; Majima et al., 2000).
 One way to overcome stress shielding is to take advantage of stress relaxation within the tendon
 (Atkinson et al., 1999). Stress relaxation is a fundamental property of viscoelastic tissues like tendons,
 where force within a tendon decreases over time when a static load is applied and the tendon is held at a
 constant length(Atkinson et al., 1999). Essentially, this means that when a tendon is loaded using isometric
 contractions the collagen fibers/fibrils/fascicles progressively relax over time, eventually reaching a steady
Downloaded by t_lambrinides@yahoo.com on 11/16/18
 state. As the collagen fibers/fibrils/fascicles relax, stress shielding within the tendon should decrease and
 a directional mechanical signal should be imparted to the injured region. Consistent with this hypothesis,
 isometric loading protocols decrease pain in high level athletes with tendinopathies (Rio et al., 2015; van
 Ark et al., 2016); however, whether a consistent program of isometric loading can improve the quality of
 the injured tendon has yet to be demonstrated.
 On top of the positive effects of loading on tendon health, we have recently shown that nutrition
 can positively affect collagen synthesis in musculoskeletal tissues (Shaw et al., 2017). Briefly, we
 demonstrated that supplementing with 15 grams of gelatin, one hour before loading, resulted in an
 increase in whole body collagen synthesis and increased mechanics and collagen content of human
 engineered ligaments (Shaw et al., 2017). These data suggest that supplementing with gelatin can increase
 collagen synthesis. Improving collagen synthesis in stress shielded tendon might be important since
 immobilization for even short periods (10 days) has been shown to reduce tendon collagen synthesis by
 up to 50% and the decline in collagen synthesis continues out to 23 days (de Boer et al., 2007). Even
 though the decrease in collagen synthesis was not associated with a decrease in patellar tendon cross-
  “Stress Relaxation and Targeted Nutrition to Treat Patellar Tendinopathy” by Baar K
 International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism
 © 2018 Human Kinetics, Inc.
 sectional area, the tendon did show decreased functional performance (de Boer et al., 2007), suggesting
 that decreased collagen synthesis is associated with impaired tendon function.
 This paper, presents a case study of a professional basketball player with chronic patellar
 tendinopathy. The player was placed on a program that combined gelatin ingestion and stress relaxation
 loading as part of a rehabilitation protocol. Of note, even with an extensive playing and training schedule,
 the protocol significantly decreased MRI reactivity, increased the thickness of the mid-substance of the
 patellar tendon, and diminished pain. The loading and nutrition protocol presented here therefore could
 be one component of a rehabilitation protocol to improve functional outcomes in elite athletes.
 Player and imaging
Downloaded by t_lambrinides@yahoo.com on 11/16/18
 As part of the NBA scouting combine, all players invited to the event are given an MRI of both
 knees. For the athlete in question, one of his knees showed significant MRI reactivity at the inferior pole
 of the patella and MRI reactivity throughout the length of the tendon that was visible both in the sagittal
 T1-weighted images (Figure 1A) and axial PDW SPectral Attenuated Inversion Recovery (SPAIR) images
 (Figure 2A). At the time, the player was 21 years old and had experienced knee pain for ~5 years. The
 initial MRI was completed in May and the player was drafted that year and began working with the team
 3 months later. Follow up MRIs were performed on a Philips Ingenia 3.0T MR system in August (Figures
 1B and 2B) of the following year (15 months after the initial scan) and six months later (February of his
 second year in the league; Figures 1C and 2C) to gauge his progression. The initial MRI was completed on
 a separate machine, but great care was used to validate that equivalent images in the original and follow
 up scans were used for comparison. In the sections shown, the same cut was used and the patellar and
 tibial areas were similar.
  “Stress Relaxation and Targeted Nutrition to Treat Patellar Tendinopathy” by Baar K
 International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism
 © 2018 Human Kinetics, Inc.
 Overview of interventions
 After being informed of the purpose of the study and of all associated risks, the player gave written
 consent. The study was performed in accordance with the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki
 and the University of California Davis Institutional Review Board.
 In-Season Loading Volume
 As the player was part of the active team, he participated in more than 50 games per season across two
 season averaging more than 20 minutes per contest. On top of game loading, he also participated in an
 average of 3 organized practices per week as well as a structured strength training program overseen by
 an elite strength and conditioning coach while being monitored by a rehabilitation specialist,
Downloaded by t_lambrinides@yahoo.com on 11/16/18
 physiotherapist, and sport medicine doctor.
 Stress Relaxation Loading
 The patellar tendon targeted training program consisted of mid-range isometric holds for 2 open
 chain (leg extension, and leg press) and one closed chain (Spanish squats) exercise. Both the weight lifted
 and the duration of the isometric hold progressively increased over the 18 months in the program. The
 isometric holds started at 10 seconds and progressively increased by 5 seconds and reached a peak of 30
 seconds 6 months into the program. The stress relaxation program was performed twice a week through
 pre-season, in-season, and off-season workouts. The athlete was asked to perform 1-3 sets of 2-4
 repetitions of single leg, mid-range isometric holds for leg extension, leg press, or Spanish squats. The
 holds were performed at >80% of 1 repetition max (1RM) and 1RM was evaluated every other month. The
 30 second isometric holds were used because the force in patellar tendon sections drops by 60% by 30
 seconds with only a further 10% decrease by 180 seconds (Atkinson et al., 1999). The length of the session
 (~10 minutes from start to finish) was used because we had previously found that short periods of loading
  “Stress Relaxation and Targeted Nutrition to Treat Patellar Tendinopathy” by Baar K
 International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism
 © 2018 Human Kinetics, Inc.
 (5-10 minutes) were optimal for stimulating the cellular response to load and increasing collagen synthesis
 (Paxton et al., 2012).
 Nutrition intervention
 Normal dietary intake for the player was not tracked, nor did the player report changes in dietary
 intake over the length of the study. One hour before the patellar tendon targeted training program, the
 athlete consumed 15 grams of gelatin with ~225 mg vitamin C. The supplement consisted of commercial
 baking gelatin (Great Lakes unflavored beef gelatin) in 16oz of orange juice (containing ~225mg vitamin
 C). The amount of gelatin was based on our previous work showing that 15 grams of gelatin increased
 load-dependent collagen synthesis (Shaw et al., 2017). The timing of nutrients prior to exercise was
Downloaded by t_lambrinides@yahoo.com on 11/16/18
 designed to enhance nutrient delivery to the injured tendon and take advantage of cellular processes
 activated by the exercise stimulus to maximize collagen synthesis.
 Compliance with the loading and nutrition program was greater than 95% in season and because
 of the early success the athlete maintained approximately this level of compliance in the offseason.
 Body Composition Assessment
 The player underwent body composition assessment via surface anthropometry using the sum of
 seven skinfolds at regular intervals throughout the program.
 Strength Assessment
 Isometric strength was determined using a Cybex 6000 isokinetic dynamometer calibrated before
 and after each test according to the manual.
 Outcome of the intervention
 Changes in body composition over the season (Table 1)
 Over the course of the season, the player saw minimal changes in body mass (-2.5kg). The
 decrease in body weight corresponded with a decrease in fat mass (from 8.4% to 5.9%), indicating that a
  “Stress Relaxation and Targeted Nutrition to Treat Patellar Tendinopathy” by Baar K
 International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism
 © 2018 Human Kinetics, Inc.
 large percentage of the body mass loss was the result of a decrease in fat mass. In agreement with this
 assessment, lean mass changed slightly over the testing period (75.6kg at the time of the initial MRI and
 74.7kg at the time of the third MRI).
 Functional progression through the program
 In spite of a slight decrease in lean mass, maximal single leg isometric hamstring strength
 increased 196%, isometric leg extension strength increased by 156% and leg press strength increased
 187.5% over the period of the program. The stress relaxation sets performed in each session for single
 legged isometric leg extensions progressed from 3 repetitions of 10 seconds with 12.5kg to 2 repetitions
 of 30 seconds with 32kg, whereas the single legged isometric leg press progressed from three 10 second
Downloaded by t_lambrinides@yahoo.com on 11/16/18
 holds with 80kg to two 30 second holds with 170kg.
 Imaging and pain
 Follow up MRI images were performed after a year in the program (15 months after the first MRI)
 and a further 6 months later, after the player had been on the program for ~18 months. The MRI images
 following 12 and 18 months into the program showed a progressive decrease in MRI reactivity at the
 inferior pole of the patella in both the sagittal T1 weighted images (Figure 1) and the axial SPAIR images
 (Figure 2). At the time of the third scan, a blinded orthopedic surgeon declared the patellar tendon normal.
 The reduction of reactivity at the inferior pole of the patella was accompanied by a decrease in the
 diameter of the patellar tendon at the proximal enthesis from 10.8mm at scan 1 to 8.7 and 8.16mm in
 scans 2 and 3, respectively. The decrease in the thickness of the proximal end of the patellar tendon was
 accompanied by an increase in the thickness at the mid-point of the tendon. The diameter of the midpoint
 of the patellar tendon progressively increased from 5.74 (scan 1), to 6.16 (scan 2) and then 6.29 (scan 3)
 mm and this was accompanied by a decrease in T1 and T2 reactivity (not shown). Therefore, the proximal
 end of the tendon decreased ~25%, whereas the middle of the tendon hypertrophied ~10%. Beyond the
  “Stress Relaxation and Targeted Nutrition to Treat Patellar Tendinopathy” by Baar K
 International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism
 © 2018 Human Kinetics, Inc.
 changes in imaging, self-reported pain and tenderness within the tendon decreased. At the point of the
 final scan, the athlete was pain free, even though he was playing more than 25 minutes a game.
 Reflections
 The goal of this case study was to determine whether a targeted loading and nutritional program
 could enhance outcomes of a patellar tendinopathy rehabilitation program. Specifically, we used a loading
 program that maximized stress relaxation (long isometric holds) in the hopes of providing a uniaxial tensile
 load to the injured region of the patellar tendon. Together with the stress relaxation loading, we primed
 the athlete with 15 grams of gelatin containing 225mg of vitamin C so that once the cells were activated
 by the load they had would have the substrates necessary to increase collagen synthesis. The major results
Downloaded by t_lambrinides@yahoo.com on 11/16/18
 of the program were a decrease in pain and tenderness that corresponded with a significant decrease in
 MRI reactivity at the inferior pole of the patella and an increase in mid-substance patellar tendon
 thickness.
 Stress relaxation is a fundamental property of viscoelastic materials like tendons and ligaments
 (Kjaer, 2004). Basically, as the tissue is loaded water is squeezed out and structures, such as fascicles and
 sub-fascicular components of the tendon slide relative to each other resulting in a progressive decrease
 in the tension within the tendon at a given length (Atkinson et al., 1999; Magnusson et al., 1997). In the
 human patellar tendon, two important observations about stress relaxation were first made by Atkinson
 and her colleagues (Atkinson et al., 1999). First, stress relaxation is bigger when larger parts of a tendon
 are loaded. This is important since it suggests that intrinsic differences in the strength of different fascicle
 or sub-fascicle regions are exposed during stress relaxation. In the current case, this is potentially
 important since it suggests that stronger regions of the tendon may relax early in the process and
 weaker/damaged regions of the tendon may be forced to take on more of the load as stress relaxation
 progresses. Since directional loading is fundamentally required for high degrees of collagen synthesis and
 matrix alignment (Kapacee et al., 2008), this suggests that stress relaxation can be used to provide a
  “Stress Relaxation and Targeted Nutrition to Treat Patellar Tendinopathy” by Baar K
 International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism
 © 2018 Human Kinetics, Inc.
 tensile stimulus to damaged regions of the collagen matrix to promote directional collagen synthesis. The
 second important observation by Atkinson and colleagues (Atkinson et al., 1999) was that stress-
 relaxation reaches ~60% within 30 seconds and continues only a further 10% more up to 180 seconds.
 This suggests that heavy isometric holds lasting 30 seconds will be sufficient to provide a similar degree
 of stress relaxation as holds lasting 6-times longer. Therefore, the rationale for the loading paradigm was
 to use stress relaxation to provide a tensile load to the cells within the damaged central core of the
 proximal patellar tendon.
 As important as tensile loading is to collagen synthesis, recent work from our group (Shaw et al.,
 2017) and others (Clark et al., 2008; McAlindon et al., 2011; Oesser et al., 1999) suggests that collagen
Downloaded by t_lambrinides@yahoo.com on 11/16/18
 synthesis can be enhanced by supplementing the diet with gelatin or hydrolyzed collagen. Specifically, we
 have previously shown that providing 15 grams of gelatin together with ~50mg of vitamin C an hour before
 loading resulted in an increase in collagen synthesis relative to a placebo or 5-gram dose of gelatin (Shaw
 et al., 2017). Therefore, for this case study we had the athlete consume 15 grams of gelatin within an
 orange juice slurry (containing ~225mg of vitamin C) one hour before the stress relaxation training. Even
 though we do not have a control group for this intervention, we have growing evidence that specific amino
 acids within the gelatin provide a stimulus to the cells of a tendon or ligament to increase collagen
 synthesis. Coupled with the directional tensile load, the added amino acids may be necessary to support
 the increase in collagen synthesis. However, much more work is needed before we can definitively
 understand the role of gelatin in the recovery described in this case study.
 As with any intervention with elite athletes, the intervention can only be effective if there is buy
 in from the player. In this case, the injury was sufficiently painful that the player was willing to drink the
 slurry and perform the loading paradigm twice a week. When the treatment showed success, the player
 quickly became a major advocate of the program within the team. Currently, any player with symptoms
 of patellar or other forms of tendinopathy quickly opts into the program and now most members of the
  “Stress Relaxation and Targeted Nutrition to Treat Patellar Tendinopathy” by Baar K
 International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism
 © 2018 Human Kinetics, Inc.
 team preform a form of prehab using the gelatin and stress relaxation loading along with their regular
 training. Even though we have not quantified musculoskeletal injuries before and after the intervention,
 reports suggest that visits to the training room and non-contact musculoskeletal injuries within the team
 have dropped.
 Tendinopathies are multifactorial in nature and central core tendinopathies are particularly
 difficult to prevent and treat in an elite population. We hope that the program reported here can provide
 a starting place for treating these debilitating injuries.

 "id":"Q22",
 "sourceFile":"Structural brain differences in professional Australian rules footballers following mild traumatic brain injury - When head size matters.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text ('Structural brain differences in professional Australian rules footballers following mild traumatic brain injury: When head size matters', Front Neurol) matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Case-control Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Brain Health & Psychology",
 "domains":["Brain Health & Psychology","Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["Other Sport"],
 "populations":["Professional / Elite","Male Athletes","Injured Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Case-control MRI study of 31 male professional Australian rules footballers scanned within 3 months of a suspected concussion (17 scanned within 12 days, 14 later) and 37 healthy male non-athlete controls matched for age. Players had lower proportional hippocampal and amygdala volumes than controls, and the bilateral hippocampal differences stayed significant after Bonferroni correction. Players also had lower right lateral orbitofrontal cortical thickness (an exploratory finding). Results depended on the intracranial volume method: only the right hippocampus differed when volumes were normalized to segmentation-based or supratentorial volume. In 12 players with follow-up scans, no subcortical volume changed significantly after correction.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Controls were non-athletes and players had unknown prior concussion history, so injury and sport exposure cannot be separated. Most ROI results are uncorrected p-values and depend on the choice of intracranial volume estimate, and the longitudinal subset was only 12 players.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the smaller hippocampus as proof that concussion causes lasting brain damage or future neurodegeneration. The design cannot show that the difference came from injury rather than pre-existing or sport-related differences, and the authors show the result changes with the head-size method used.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2026,
   "citation":"Lee JM, Pardoe HR, Parker DM, Pedersen M, Makdissi M, Abbott DF, et al. Structural brain differences in professional Australian rules footballers following mild traumatic brain injury: When head size matters. Front Neurol. 2026;17:1701097.",
   "doi":"10.3389/fneur.2026.1701097",
   "abstract":"Quantified subcortical and cortical structural MRI differences between 31 recently concussed professional Australian rules footballers and 37 healthy non-athlete controls. Footballers had lower proportional hippocampal and amygdala volumes and reduced cortical thickness, but the volumetric findings depended on the intracranial volume estimation method used for normalization.",
   "tldr":"Recently concussed professional footballers had smaller hippocampal volumes than non-athlete controls, but the result depends on how head size is estimated. It is a useful cross-sectional signal, not a diagnostic or return-to-play marker.",
   "methods":"Retrospective case-control study of 31 professional male footballers scanned within 3 months of a suspected concussion (acute group 17, sub-acute group 14) and 37 healthy male controls. T1-weighted 3 T MRI was processed with FreeSurfer recon-all, and hippocampal and amygdala volumes were normalized to estimated total intracranial volume (eTIV). Vertex-wise cortical thickness and a subset of 12 players with follow-up scans were also analyzed, and two other intracranial volume estimates were compared as an exploratory step.",
   "findings":"Players had lower proportional bilateral hippocampal and amygdala volumes than controls at uncorrected p < 0.05, with the bilateral hippocampal differences remaining significant after Bonferroni correction. Players had a cluster of lower right lateral orbitofrontal cortical thickness (peak p = 0.013, exploratory). Players had larger eTIV than controls (p < 0.001). When normalized to segmentation-based total intracranial volume or supratentorial volume, only the right hippocampus differed. In 12 players with follow-up scans, no subcortical volume changed after correction, and a right hippocampal reduction (p = 0.042) did not survive correction. In an exploratory analysis of 25 players, smaller left hippocampal volume correlated with poorer CogSport learning scores (r = 0.44, p = 0.030).",
   "limitations":"The cohort is male and all players were professionals, and controls were non-athletes, so sport exposure, head size and injury history are confounded. Prior concussion history was not known. Most ROI results are uncorrected, and the choice of intracranial volume method changed which findings held. The longitudinal sample was small, the cognitive correlations were exploratory, and two scanner models were used.",
   "practicalImplications":"Staff interpreting hippocampal or amygdala volume results after concussion should check how intracranial volume was normalized, and should not treat a single MRI volume as evidence of injury or of a future problem. Clinical use needs a larger study with athlete controls and pre-injury baselines.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: The study does not measure sport performance. Its only performance-adjacent finding is an exploratory link between smaller left hippocampal volume and poorer learning scores in a subset of players, which is not a basis for selection or training decisions.",
   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: The study does not link MRI volumes to return-to-play timing, and it cannot be used to clear or hold a player. Most scans were taken within weeks of injury, and no recovery outcome was tied to the volume measures."
 }
}

Keywords: Introduction: After mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI), the brain is labile for weeks and months and vulnerable to
Concussion repeated concussions. During this time, patients are exposed to everyday circumstances that, in themselves,
Repeated mild traumatic brain injury affect brain metabolism and blood flow and neural processing. How commonplace activities interact with the
Postconcussion syndrome
 injured brain is unknown. The present study in an animal model investigated the extent to which three
Functional magnetic resonance imaging
 commonly experienced exposures—daily caffeine usage, chronic sleep loss, and chronic sleep aid medi­
Diffusion tensor imaging
Regional homogeneity cation—affect the injured brain in the chronic phase.
Sleep deficiency Methods: Subclinical trauma by repeated mTBIs was produced by our head rotational acceleration injury model,
Caffeine which causes brain injury consistent with the mechanism of concussion in humans. Forty-eight hours after a third
Sleep aids mTBI, chronic administrations of caffeine, sleep restriction, or zolpidem (sedative hypnotic) began and were
Zolpidem continued for 70 days. On Days 30 and 60 post injury, resting state functional magnetic resonance imaging
Animal models (fMRI) and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) were performed.
 Results: Chronic caffeine, sleep restriction, and zolpidem each changed the subclinical brain characteristics of
 mTBI at both 30 and 60 days post injury, detected by different MRI modalities. Each treatment caused micro­
 structural alterations in DTI metrics in the insular cortex and retrosplenial cortex compared with mTBI, but also
 uniquely affected other gray and white matter regions. Zolpidem administration affected the largest number of
 individual structures in mTBI at both 30 and 60 days, and not necessarily toward normalization (sham treat­
 ment). Chronic sleep restriction changed local functional connectivity at 30 days in diametrical opposition to
 chronic caffeine ingestion, and both treatment outcomes were different from sham, mTBI-only and zolpidem
 comparisons. The results indicate that commonly encountered exposures modify subclinical brain activity and
 structure long after healing is expected to be complete.
 Conclusions: Changes in activity and structure detected by fMRI are widely understood to reflect changes in the
 functions of the affected region which conceivably underlie mTBI neuropathology and symptomatology in the
 chronic phase after injury.
